title: Your First 90 Days of Freelancing: What to Realistically Expect
description: What the first 90 days of freelancing usually look like: a slow first month, platform fees, a sample income breakdown, and how to get your first client.

cover.alt: A desk with a three-month calendar and plants growing taller in three pots

takeaways: Month one is mostly unpaid setup and pitching. That is normal, not a sign it isn't working.
Platforms take a cut. Fiverr keeps 20% and Upwork charges up to 15%, so price with the fee included.

body:
Most stories about starting freelancing are told by people it worked out for, looking back. They skip the part where nothing happens for weeks.

This is the version for someone about to start. It covers what the first 90 days usually involve, what the platforms take, and a sample breakdown so you can see how the numbers behave. The sample is an illustration built to show the maths. It is not anyone's real income report, and yours will differ.

## Before day one: three decisions

1. **One skill, described in one sentence.** "I edit short videos for fitness coaches" gets replies. "I can do anything" doesn't. If you haven't picked a skill, start with these [online skills worth learning](/blog/best-online-skills-to-learn-for-income/).
2. **Three samples.** Nobody hires a blank profile. Make three pieces that look like paid work, even if nobody paid for them.
3. **A weekly time budget.** Decide your hours, for example eight a week, and protect them. Freelancing done "when I have time" rarely gets done.

## Days 1 to 30: setup and silence

The first month is mostly unpaid. You build a profile, write samples, learn how the platform works and send pitches that go unanswered.

What to do:

- **Pitch every working day.** Five short, specific pitches beat one long perfect one.
- **Keep each pitch to a few lines.** Say what you noticed about their project, what you'd do, and link one relevant sample.
- **Take a small first job.** A low-paid job with a good review is worth more this month than holding out for your ideal rate.
- **Tell people you know.** Many first clients come from a friend of a friend, not a marketplace.

What it feels like: discouraging. Most pitches get no reply at all. That is how it works for nearly everyone at the start.

## Days 31 to 60: first clients, first lessons

Somewhere in the second month, the first proper jobs tend to arrive. They bring lessons no course covers.

- **Scope creep.** "Can you just also..." Decide what is included before you start, in writing.
- **Slow replies.** Clients take days to answer. Keep pitching while you wait.
- **Underpricing.** You will quote too low at least once. Note how long the job really took and adjust the next quote.

Ask every happy client for two lines of feedback. Reviews are what make month three easier than month one.

## Days 61 to 90: repeat work

The real change in the third month is not more pitches. It is that an earlier client comes back, or sends someone your way.

- **Offer a next step.** When you deliver, suggest what you could do next. "I can do four of these a month for a fixed price" turns one job into regular work.
- **Raise your rate for new clients.** Keep existing clients where they are for now and quote higher to new ones.
- **Drop what doesn't pay.** If a type of job always takes twice as long as you expected, stop taking it.

## What the platforms take

Marketplaces find you clients and charge for the service. Know the numbers before you set a price.

| Platform | Fee taken from the freelancer |
|---|---|
| Fiverr | A flat 20% of what you earn |
| Upwork | A service fee of 0% to 15%, depending on the work |

On Fiverr, a $100 job pays you $80. If you need $100 in hand, you have to charge $125. Upwork also uses "Connects", credits you spend to apply for jobs. Its basic plan may include a few free ones each month.

Fees and plans change, so check each platform's current terms.

## A sample 90-day breakdown

Here is an illustration for a beginner working around eight hours a week on a platform that takes 20%. The figures are invented to show how the first quarter typically moves. They are not a promise and not a real person's results.

| Measure | Month 1 | Month 2 | Month 3 | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hours worked (including pitching) | 30 | 34 | 38 | 102 |
| Paying clients | 1 | 2 | 3 | |
| Income before fees | $80 | $260 | $520 | $860 |
| Platform fee (20%) | $16 | $52 | $104 | $172 |
| Income after fees | $64 | $208 | $416 | $688 |
| Real hourly rate | $2.13 | $6.12 | $10.95 | $6.75 |

Three things to notice:

- **Month one looks terrible.** $64 for 30 hours. Most of those hours were setup and pitching, which you only do once at that intensity.
- **The trend matters more than the total.** The hourly rate climbs from about $2 to about $11 as paid work replaces unpaid pitching.
- **Fees are real money.** $172 of the $860 never reached the freelancer.

When you track your own first 90 days, use the same rows. Count every hour, including the ones spent applying. That is the only way to know your real rate.

## Mistakes that slow beginners down

- **Offering everything to everyone.** A narrow offer is easier to find and easier to trust.
- **Copy-pasting the same pitch.** Clients can tell. Two specific lines about their project beat a paragraph about you.
- **Quitting in week three.** The silence at the start is normal. Give it the full 90 days before you judge.
- **Forgetting tax.** Freelance income is usually taxable. Keep a record of every payment and set a share aside. The rules depend on your country.
- **Spending it before it clears.** Platforms often hold payments for days or weeks.

## Is freelancing worth it for you?

After 90 days, ask three questions:

1. Is my real hourly rate rising month to month?
2. Has at least one client come back or referred someone?
3. Do I still want to do this work?

Two yeses is a reason to continue. If the answer to all three is no, you have lost a few months and gained a skill, a portfolio and a clearer idea of what you don't want. That isn't a bad trade.

## What to do with the first income

Irregular income needs a plan more than a salary does. Budget from your lowest month, not your best one, as explained in [how to budget on a low income](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/). And send part of every payment to an [emergency fund](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/), because freelance months are uneven by nature.

If you are a student and want something smaller to begin with, these [side hustles need no money to start](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/).
